claims.text: Severe sliding contact induces an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer through dynamic amorphization in coarse-grained CoCrFeMnNi.
The sliding-induced ultra-nanocrystalline layer is associated with low friction under inert ultra-high-vacuum conditions.
The sliding-induced ultra-nanocrystalline layer is associated with very low wear under inert conditions.
Fine grains and residual stress weaken the passive layer and reduce the corrosion resistance of Cantor alloys.
The high grain-boundary and defect density of the sliding-induced layer disrupts the integrity of the passive film.
Disruption of the passive film exposes additional electrochemically active sites to the electrolyte.
The sliding-induced refined layer causes accelerated localized corrosion.
Accelerated corrosion couples synergistically with wear and dominates overall degradation.
The proposed starting material is a coarse-grained, single-phase CoCrFeMnNi Cantor alloy.
The starting Cantor alloy has an established, stable passive film in the absence of severe deformation.
Applying identical load and sliding speed in inert and NaCl environments will produce similar strain rates and surface grain refinement.
A 3.5 wt% NaCl environment invokes simultaneous corrosion during sliding.
An ultra-high-vacuum or argon sliding test provides a wear-only baseline in which oxidation and oxide-film formation are suppressed.
The nanocrystalline layer lowers shear strength and accommodates interfacial shear.
Relative to inert sliding, sliding in NaCl will produce higher total degradation.
The mechanical wear component in NaCl may be lower than the inert baseline because of grain refinement.
The corrosion component in NaCl will increase because the refined microstructure has poorer passive-film stability.
The prediction applies only when sliding-induced nanocrystallization occurs and passive-film formation is sensitive to microstructural refinement.
The mechanism may fail in alloys with exceptionally robust passive films or when corrosion kinetics are insensitive to grain-boundary density.
Absence of both statistically significant passive-film degradation and increased total degradation in the corrosive test would falsify the proposed coupling mechanism.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as an inert environment in which a continuous passive oxide film is present, while the inert UHV/argon condition is also described as suppressing oxidation and mixed oxide-film formation. It is therefore unclear whether the baseline is intended to retain a passive film or to eliminate oxide-film effects.

The intervention assumes similar strain rates and grain refinement in both environments, but the predicted lower mechanical wear in the corrosive test is attributed to grain refinement. A mediator expected in both arms cannot by itself explain a difference between them.
